title: Recursion in three rounds
description: Round 1: see calls descend and return. Round 2: write shrinking-window and nested-container recursions. Round 3: trace branches, reuse states, measure work, and transfer the idea.

learned: Justify a base case with a decreasing argument on the allowed domain.
Distinguish call occurrences from distinct subproblem states.
Reuse completed states without confusing a cache with stack removal.
Choose a dependency order that supports large Python inputs.
recap.invariant: Each completed stored state has the correct answer; earlier dependencies are available before a new state is completed.
recap.complexity: Count transitions and recurrence additions, not elapsed time. Memoized routes expand at most n positive states; ordered packing uses at most n times the number of allowed sizes additions, with modular residues and drawing excluded.
recap.common_mistake: Assuming that memoization or a tail-position call removes Python recursion depth.
in_real_programs: Python exposes a recursion-depth limit; raising it does not remove recursive stack growth.

retrieval.question: Module 2: why can separate calls use the same parameter name independently?
retrieval.answer: Each invocation has its own local parameter binding; the same spelling does not imply the same binding.

exercises.title: Build: draw pending recursive work
exercises.prompt_md: Repair `recursive_sum(n, stack=None)` for nonnegative integers up to 20. It must recursively call itself with n minus one and return the sum from 1 through n. Start a fresh stack when none is supplied, append the current n, then call `show_stack("enter", stack, n)`. Before removing that n, call `show_stack("leave", stack, result)` with its actual returned answer. Record the base call too. A supplied stack must be restored on return; do not keep state between invocations.

checklist.step: Recurse to zero with fresh state and correct answers
Show descent and return answers in the real stack

exercises.starter_code:
def recursive_sum(n,stack=None):
    if stack is None:stack=[]
    stack.append(n)
    show_stack("enter",stack,n)
    result=n  # include the smaller recursive answer
    show_stack("leave",stack,result)
    stack.pop()
    return result
from scimigo import canvas,figure,frame,text

def show_stack(stage,stack,result):
    canvas(600,300)
    figure("array_state",x=0,y=0,width=600,height=240,
           values=list(stack),indices=False)
    text(12,275,stage+": "+str(result),size=18)
    frame()

print(recursive_sum(3))

def recursive_sum(n,stack=None):
    if stack is None:stack=[]
    stack.append(n)

    show_stack("leave",stack,result)
    stack.pop()
    return result

exercises.title: Round 2: move two boundaries
exercises.prompt_md: Implement mirrored(items, left=0, right=None) for lists of integers with at most 20 elements. Compare the current outside pair; if it matches, recursively check only the inside window. An empty or one-element window is mirrored. Do not slice or mutate the input. Call show_window on entry with answer None and before return with the Boolean answer. Use the same original list in every frame. Defaults select the whole list; explicit boundaries select an inclusive valid subwindow.

checklist.step: Check the inside and preserve the input
Show each shrinking window and returning answer

exercises.starter_code:
def mirrored(items,left=0,right=None):
    if right is None:right=len(items)-1
    show_window(items,left,right,"enter",None)
    answer=True if left>=right else items[left]==items[right]
    # Matching outside values are not enough: check the inside too.
    show_window(items,left,right,"leave",answer)
    return answer
from scimigo import canvas,figure,frame,text

def show_window(items,left,right,stage,answer):
    canvas(600,300)
    figure("array_state",x=0,y=0,width=600,height=220,
           values=list(items),indices=True,
           highlights={str(i):"current" for i in range(max(0,left),min(len(items),right+1))},
           pointers=[{"index":left,"label":"left","position":"above"},
                     {"index":right,"label":"right","position":"below"}])
    text(12,250,"left="+str(left)+"  right="+str(right)+"  "+stage,size=18)
    text(12,280,"answer="+str(answer),size=18)
    frame()

print(mirrored([4,7,2,7,4]))

exercises.solution:
def mirrored(items,left=0,right=None):
    if right is None:right=len(items)-1
    show_window(items,left,right,"enter",None)
    if left>=right:
        answer=True
    elif items[left]!=items[right]:
        answer=False
    else:
        answer=mirrored(items,left+1,right-1)
    show_window(items,left,right,"leave",answer)
    return answer
from scimigo import canvas,figure,frame,text

def show_window(items,left,right,stage,answer):
    canvas(600,300)
    figure("array_state",x=0,y=0,width=600,height=220,
           values=list(items),indices=True,
           highlights={str(i):"current" for i in range(max(0,left),min(len(items),right+1))},
           pointers=[{"index":left,"label":"left","position":"above"},
                     {"index":right,"label":"right","position":"below"}])
    text(12,250,"left="+str(left)+"  right="+str(right)+"  "+stage,size=18)
    text(12,280,"answer="+str(answer),size=18)
    frame()

print(mirrored([4,7,2,7,4]))

exercises.title: Round 2: combine nested children
exercises.prompt_md: Implement nested_total(node, path=()) for finite acyclic lists containing integers or more lists, with nesting depth at most 10. Integers return themselves; an empty list returns zero; other lists combine the answers from all children. Recursively visit children left to right. Append each child index to its tuple path. Call show_node(path, node, answer) once after this node is complete, including leaves and empty lists. Do not mutate input or keep an accumulator between calls.

checklist.step: Visit nested and empty containers without mutation

exercises.starter_code:
def nested_total(node,path=()):
    if isinstance(node,int):
        answer=node
    else:
        answer=sum(child for child in node if isinstance(child,int))
        # Nested children contribute too; visit each one separately.
    show_node(path,node,answer)
    return answer
from scimigo import canvas,figure,frame,text

def show_node(path,node,answer):
    canvas(600,300)
    figure("array_state",x=0,y=0,width=600,height=220,
           values=["integer" if isinstance(node,int) else "list",answer],
           cell_width=110,indices=False)
    text(12,260,"completed path="+str(path),size=18)
    frame()

print(nested_total([3,[2,[],[5]],1]))

exercises.solution:
def nested_total(node,path=()):
    if isinstance(node,int):
        answer=node
    else:
        answer=0
        for i,child in enumerate(node):
            answer+=nested_total(child,path+(i,))
    show_node(path,node,answer)
    return answer
from scimigo import canvas,figure,frame,text

    canvas(600,300)
    figure("array_state",x=0,y=0,width=600,height=220,
           values=["integer" if isinstance(node,int) else "list",answer],
           cell_width=110,indices=False)
    text(12,260,"completed path="+str(path),size=18)
    frame()

exercises.prompt_md: Complete `route_trace(n)` for routes made of jumps of length 1 or 3, where order matters. Zero remaining distance has one completed route; negative remaining distance has none. For positive n, add the counts of the two smaller remainders. After its children finish, every call invokes `show_route(n, result)` once, including zero and negative base calls. Evaluate the length-1 child before the length-3 child. Demo n is 4. Predict the total call occurrences, including the original and all base calls; the picture records completion order.

exercises.title: Implement: compute each state once
exercises.prompt_md: Repair `memo_routes(n)` for nonnegative n up to 200. It counts ordered routes with jumps 1 or 3. The supplied `transition(k)` returns the two dependencies. Call it exactly once for each positive state expanded, never for a base state. Reuse a completed state within one invocation; start fresh between invocations. Record each newly completed positive state with `record_state(k, value)` exactly once. Zero returns one and negative dependencies return zero. The starter repeats solved work.

checklist.step: Compute correct routes with one expansion per positive state
Draw every newly completed positive state once

exercises.starter_code:
def memo_routes(n):
    def solve(k):
        if k<0:return 0
        if k==0:return 1
        left,right=transition(k)
        value=solve(left)+solve(right)
        record_state(k,value)
        return value
    return solve(n)
from scimigo import canvas,figure,frame,text

def transition(k):
    return k-1,k-3

def record_state(k,value):
    canvas(600,280)
    figure("array_state",x=0,y=0,width=600,height=230,
           values=[k,value],indices=False)
    text(12,260,"Stored state "+str(k)+": "+str(value),size=18)
    frame()

print(memo_routes(4))

exercises.title: Mastery challenge: ordered packing plans
exercises.prompt_md: A packing line fills exactly n units using permitted batch sizes. Order matters: a small batch followed by a larger one is a different plan from the reverse. Implement `packing_plans(n, sizes, modulus)` returning the number of plans modulo a positive integer. The sizes are distinct positive integers in any order, and n is nonnegative. Zero units has one empty plan; no permitted sizes means no plan for positive n. Use `combine(a, b, modulus)` for each addition of plan counts. For n up to 6,000, use at most n times the number of sizes combine calls and avoid a deep Python call chain. Settings and counts must be fresh between calls. The starter follows valid smaller remainders but repeats work and cannot support the large request. The demo displays the residue actually returned.

questions.prompt: What must be true before a count is completed?

choices.text: Every dependency has a completed answer
choices.why: Only completed smaller answers may be combined.

choices.text: Only the largest batch is considered
choices.why: That discards plans using other permitted batches.

choices.text: The final residue is already known
choices.why: That restates the output without explaining correctness.

questions.prompt: Which property makes reused answers valid?

choices.text: All settings share one count table
choices.why: Different sizes or moduli can change the answer.

choices.text: Earlier answers match this request's rules
choices.why: The same batch choices and modulus determine each stored answer.

choices.text: Every remainder has exactly one plan
choices.why: Several ordered plans can fill the same remainder.

questions.prompt: Which bound fits n units and k permitted batch sizes?

choices.why: The specified process must combine preceding states.

choices.text: At most n times k additions
choices.why: For each positive amount, there is at most one addition per permitted batch size.

questions.prompt: With sizes 1 and 2, how many ordered plans fill 3 units?

choices.why: This merges [1,2] and [2,1], contrary to the order-sensitive contract.
There is no fourth plan with only positive sizes 1 and 2.

checklist.step: Count ordered plans with varied settings and edge cases
Meet the addition budget and handle large Python inputs

tests.name: packing_behavior
tests.code:
import random
rng=random.Random(3003)
def oracle(n,sizes,mod):
    table=[1%mod]+[0]*n
    for k in range(1,n+1):table[k]=sum(table[k-s] for s in sizes if s<=k)%mod
    return table[n]
for _ in range(25):
    n=rng.randrange(0,9);sizes=rng.sample(range(1,7),rng.randrange(0,4));mod=rng.choice([1,2,7,97])
    old=list(sizes)
    assert packing_plans(n,sizes,mod)==oracle(n,sizes,mod),"Count ordered plans using these settings, including the empty plan."
    assert sizes==old
assert packing_plans(0,[],13)==1 and packing_plans(5,[],13)==0
assert packing_plans(3,[1,2],97)==3,"Ordered plans are [1,1,1], [1,2], and [2,1]."
